newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: World labour unions to send new team to S.Korea.
newsitem.headline: World labour unions to send new team to S.Korea.

text.p: Trade union organisations from around the world are to send their leaders to South Korea next week to observe the current strike wave in the country, a major labour federation said on Thursday.

The Geneva-based International Federation of Commercial and Clerical Workers (FIET) said the team would be headed by Bill Jordan, secretary-general of the Brussels-based International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU).

The 10-member team will replace a group of four senior union officials who were hustled out of South Korea by the authorities earlier in the day, accused of violating the law by supporting the strikers.

"The intention is to maintain an international trade union presence in Seoul at a level high enough to show the South Korean authorities this is not going to go away," FIET spokesman Nick Grisewood said.
He said the visit would be "open-ended".

The delegation, due in Seoul on Monday, would include New Zealand trade union general-secretary Ken Douglas, Vic Thorpe who heads the international chemical workers' federation, and labour leaders from several other countries.
FIET's own secretary-general, Phil Jennings, was also likely to join it.

The team forced to leave Seoul on Thursday morning included Marcello Malentacchi, leader of the Geneva-based International Metalworkers' Federation, and John Evans, head of the trade union advisory committee to the OECD.

South Korea was admitted to the OECD, the 29-member Paris- based Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, late last year after pledging to change its tough labour laws to bring them into line with international conventions.

But legislation passed on December 26 at an early morning parliamentary session kept secret from the opposition only provides for recognition of the militant Korean Confederation of Trade Unions by the year 2000.

Foreign trade unions also assert that the arrest of South Korean union leaders for organising strikes is a violation of freedoms which Seoul committed itself to observe when it joined the International Labour Organisation (ILO) in 1991.

Director-General Michel Hansenne of the ILO, a United Nations agency, warned on Thursday that there could be no solution to the industrial unrest affecting several South Korean cities over the new law unless union freedom was respected.
